## What you will do

Notebook 2 left you 400 interviewed twins. Each has a probability of voting for
Harris in 2024 and for Brown in 2026. Averaging them tells you about *these 400
twins*. **MrP** (multilevel regression and post-stratification) turns them into
an estimate for *Ohio*, and for each of its 15 districts:

1. **regress:** fit a multilevel model with the twin's answer on the left and
   who the twin is on the right. In words: P(Harris), or P(Brown), modelled on
   sex, degree, age band, ethnicity and district;
2. **post-stratify:** predict every cell of the Ohio frame and add the cells up,
   weighted by how many people the frame puts in each;
3. **validate:** compare with the certified 2024 result, district by district,
   and with the 2026 Senate polls.

You will fit two versions. **Model A** is textbook census MrP and fails at the
district level in an instructive way. **Model B** uses the stage-2 frame from
Notebook 1 and gets the districts right, for a reason you should be suspicious
of.

The last section steps back from your 400 twins to the Talking to Machines panels: twelve
of them, and a held-out election that tests what the 2024 recall cannot.

**Figure 3.1** is a reading guide for the whole notebook: what MrP does with
your twins (A), the one thing that separates the two models (B), and the three
checks, only one of which can fail (C).

**Figure 3.1.** Reading guide.

```{r reading-guide, echo = FALSE, out.width = "100%"}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path("..", "figures", "nb3_reading_guide.png"))
```

**How to read this notebook.** As in Notebooks 1 and 2, every table and figure
the code prints has a number, given in bold just above the code that prints it,
and the text says which table, row or column a number comes from.

DATA <- file.path("..", "data")

PANELS <- file.exists(file.path(DATA, "benchmark_12panels.csv"))   # Section 7: not in the public repository

## 1. Inputs

The block below loads your interviewed twins, the file Notebook 2 deposited, as
a table called `iv`, and prints its size: 400 twins, one row each, with their
skeleton, rake weight and answers.

**Table 3.1.** `iv`: size (rows, columns).

```{r twins}
iv <- as.data.table(read_parquet(file.path(OUT, "oh_mini_panel_400_interviewed.parquet")))
dim(iv)
```

```{r stub-banner, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
if (isTRUE(any(iv$stub)))
  cat("> **STAND-IN ANSWERS.** The answers loaded above were not given by a",
      "language model. A script manufactured them from each twin's 2024 vote class,",
      "so they carry that class by construction, and any model that uses the class",
      "will look good. Every number below this line only shows that the code runs.",
      "Render Notebook 2 with the cached answers to replace them.\n")
```

The **post-stratification frame** is the list of cells MrP predicts and then
adds up. It is the Notebook 1 stage-2 frame (`sf2`), collapsed to the cells your
twins carry: district × sex × ethnicity × age × degree. The block below loads
`sf2`, adds up its rows by that key into a table called `frame`, and keeps two
columns per cell: its adults (`N`) and its 2024 voters (`voters_2024`). It
prints the totals.

**Table 3.2.** `frame`: cells, adults and 2024 voters.

```{r frame}
sf2 <- as.data.table(read_parquet(file.path(DATA, "SF_extended_OH.parquet")))
frame <- sf2[, .(N = sum(N), voters_2024 = sum(N_D + N_R + N_Other)),
             by = .(cd = area, gender, ethnicity, age_bins, college_grad)]
frame <- frame[N > 0]
cat(sprintf("%s cells, %s adults, %s 2024 voters\n", format(nrow(frame), big.mark = ","),
            format(round(sum(frame$N)), big.mark = ","), format(round(sum(frame$voters_2024)), big.mark = ",")))
```

Table 3.2: 2,385 cells holding Ohio's 8,931,251 citizen adults (the figure in
Notebook 1, Table 1.2), of whom about 5.77 million voted in 2024.

From Section 5 on, the same frame is also needed split by 2024 vote class. The block
below builds that as `frame_class`: each cell of `frame` becomes four rows, one
per class (D, R, Other, stay), with the stage-2 counts `N_D`, `N_R`, `N_Other`
and `N_stay` as their `N`. It prints the adults in each class.

**Table 3.3.** `frame_class`: adults per 2024 vote class.

```{r frame-class}
frame_class <- melt(sf2, id.vars = c("area", "gender", "ethnicity", "age_bins", "college_grad"),
                    measure.vars = c("N_D", "N_R", "N_Other", "N_stay"),
                    variable.name = "vote2024", value.name = "N")
frame_class[, vote2024 := sub("^N_", "", as.character(vote2024))]
frame_class <- frame_class[N > 0, .(N = sum(N)), by = .(cd = area, gender, ethnicity, age_bins, college_grad, vote2024)]
frame_class[, .(adults = round(sum(N))), by = vote2024]
```

The benchmark is the certified 2024 result by district, from the same file as
Notebook 1, Section 3. The block below loads it as `cert` (one row per district, with
Harris's two-party share in `certified`) and computes the statewide share from
the county returns (`state_certified`, 44.3%). It prints nothing; both appear in
Tables 3.5 and 3.8.

```{r certified}
cert <- fread(file.path(DATA, "predictor_cd119_2024.csv"),
              colClasses = list(character = "CD119"))[state == "OH"]
cert <- cert[, .(cd = paste0("OH-", CD119), certified = votes_D / (votes_D + votes_R))]
state_certified <- fread(file.path(DATA, "oh_county_certified_2024.csv"))[, sum(sD * votes) / sum((sD + sR) * votes)]
```

---

## 2. The starting point: a weighted average

Notebook 2 averaged the twins with their rake weights. That is a fair statewide
number, since the weights make the 400 match the frame's margins. It is a poor
district number, because 400 twins spread over 15 districts leaves about 27 a
district.

The block below repeats that average. `voters` keeps the twins whose class is D
or R; `harris_2p` is each one's Harris share of its own Harris + Trump
probability. `raw_state` is the weighted average for Ohio, and `raw_cd` the
same average for each district. It prints the five districts with the fewest
twins.

**Table 3.4.** The weighted average by district (`raw`), for the five districts
with the fewest twins.

```{r raw}
voters <- iv[vote2024 != "stay"]
voters[, harris_2p := harris / (harris + trump)]
raw_state <- voters[, sum(weight * harris_2p) / sum(weight)]
raw_cd <- voters[, .(twins = .N, raw = sum(weight * harris_2p) / sum(weight)), by = cd]
raw_cd[order(twins)][1:5]
```

Look at the `twins` column of Table 3.4: OH-11 rests on 14 voting twins, and
the others on 16 or 17. A district estimate from so few people is noisy.

---

## 3. Model A: census MrP

The outcome is each twin's Harris probability among 2024 voters. The probability
comes from the interview in Notebook 2: each twin answered with probabilities
rather than a choice, so it enters the model as a fractional Harris vote and a
fractional Trump vote. In practice every twin enters **twice**: once as a
Harris vote with weight *p*, once as a Trump vote with weight 1 − *p*. A
logistic model fitted to these rows estimates the same thing as a model of the
probabilities themselves. `glmer` warns about non-integer weights, which is
expected here.

Model A is the textbook MrP: it uses only what the census knows about people.

- **Fixed effects** for the two-level variables, sex and degree.
- **Random intercepts** for age, ethnicity and district. A district with few
  twins is pulled towards the state average; one with more is left closer to
  its own data. This partial pooling is the "multilevel" in MrP.

The block below prints nothing. It defines `stack()`, which makes the two rows
per twin (`y = 1` weighted by *p*, `y = 0` weighted by 1 − *p*), applies it to
`voters` to build the model's data, `s24`, and defines `fit()`, the one call
that fits every model in this notebook.

```{r stack}
stack <- function(d, p, w = rep(1, nrow(d))) {
  keep <- d[, .(cd, gender, ethnicity, age_bins, college_grad, vote2024)]
  rbind(cbind(keep, y = 1L, wt = p * w), cbind(keep, y = 0L, wt = (1 - p) * w))
}
s24 <- stack(voters, voters$harris_2p)

# one fitting call for every model in this notebook; nAGQ = 0 is the fast, robust approximation
fit <- function(f, d) suppressWarnings(glmer(f, data = d, weights = wt, family = binomial, nAGQ = 0))
```

The next block fits Model A as `m_a`, prints how long it took, and prints the
standard deviation of each random intercept.

**Table 3.5.** Model A: the random-intercept standard deviations
(`Std.Dev.`), one per grouping.

```{r fit-a}
t0 <- Sys.time()
m_a <- fit(y ~ gender + college_grad + (1 | age_bins) + (1 | ethnicity) + (1 | cd), s24)
cat(sprintf("fitted in %.1f s\n", as.numeric(difftime(Sys.time(), t0, units = "secs"))))
VarCorr(m_a)
```

The random-effect standard deviations say how much each grouping matters once
the others are held fixed. Look at the `cd` (district) row of Table 3.5: its
standard deviation is 0. The model found no district differences worth keeping.

### Post-stratify

Predict every frame cell, including cells no twin sits in (`allow.new.levels`
gives them the average for that group). Then weight each cell by its **2024
voters**, and add up.

The block below does exactly that and prints nothing. It adds Model A's
predicted Harris share to every row of `frame` (column `p_a`), then averages
`p_a` weighted by `voters_2024`: by district into `a_cd`, and for Ohio into
`a_state`. Both appear in the tables below.

```{r poststrat-a}
frame[, p_a := predict(m_a, newdata = frame, type = "response", allow.new.levels = TRUE)]
a_cd <- frame[, .(model_a = sum(voters_2024 * p_a) / sum(voters_2024)), by = cd]
a_state <- frame[, sum(voters_2024 * p_a) / sum(voters_2024)]
```

---

## 4. Validate Model A, district by district

The block below joins `cert`, `raw_cd` and `a_cd` into one table, `v`, one row
per district, and prints it in percent. It then summarises each estimate's
error across the 15 districts as a root mean squared error (RMSE), in points:
the typical size of a district's miss.

**Table 3.6.** For each district: the **certified** Harris share, the plain
**weighted average** (Section 2), and **Model A**, all in percent.

**Table 3.7.** The error of each estimate across the 15 districts (RMSE, in
points).

```{r validate-a}
v <- Reduce(function(a, b) merge(a, b, by = "cd"), list(cert, raw_cd, a_cd))
v[order(cd), .(cd, twins, certified = round(100 * certified, 1), weighted_avg = round(100 * raw, 1),
               model_a = round(100 * model_a, 1))]
v[, .(rmse_weighted_avg = sqrt(mean((100 * (raw - certified))^2)),
      rmse_model_a      = sqrt(mean((100 * (model_a - certified))^2)))]
```

Model A pulls every district towards the middle, and it does *worse* than the
plain weighted average: its RMSE in Table 3.7 is about twice the weighted
average's. In Table 3.6, the strongly Democratic districts around Columbus and
Cleveland come out far too low (OH-03: certified 70.3, Model A 53.5; OH-11: 77.7
against 58.7), and the most Republican ones too high (OH-02: 26.0 against 39.9).

The reason is that Ohio's districts differ **politically**, not just
demographically. Two white, non-graduate 50-year-olds in OH-11 and OH-06 vote
differently, and the census cell cannot tell them apart. The district intercept
could in principle pick that up, but with about 27 twins a district it is shrunk
to zero (Table 3.5). Census MrP normally rescues this with a **district-level
predictor**, such as the previous election's result.

average, and are they the ones with the fewest twins? Write a block that

`model_a - raw`, in points) and prints the five largest with their `twins`.

## 5. Model B: put the vote class back

Your frame already knows each cell's 2024 politics. Stage 2 (Notebook 1, Section 2)
split every cell into D, R, other and stay-home, raked to the certified result.
Every twin carries its class, and the donor was matched on it. Model B adds the
class as a predictor and post-stratifies over **cell × vote class**, using the
stage-2 counts.

Be clear about the mechanism before you look at the result. The new predictor
is the 2024 vote class of the twin's cell, which was raked to the certified
result. The outcome is the twin's own 2024 answer, and the twin's donor was
chosen to share that same class. So the model regresses the twins' 2024 answers
on a variable those answers were built to follow. A strong fit is guaranteed by
construction.

The block below fits Model B as `m_b`: Model A plus the vote class as a fixed
effect. It prints the fixed effects.

**Table 3.8.** Model B: fixed effects, on the log-odds scale.

```{r fit-b}
m_b <- fit(y ~ gender + college_grad + vote2024 + (1 | age_bins) + (1 | ethnicity) + (1 | cd), s24)
fixef(m_b)
```

In Table 3.8, `vote2024R` is by far the largest effect: being in an R cell
rather than a D cell lowers the log-odds of a Harris answer by about 3.8.

The two-party share is about D and R voters only, so post-stratification uses
the D and R cells of the stage-2 frame. Third-party voters count for neither.

The block below keeps the D and R rows of `frame_class` as `dr`, adds Model B's
prediction to each (`p_b`), and averages it weighted by the cell's `N`: by
district into `b_cd`, and for Ohio into `b_state`. It adds Model B to `v` and
prints two tables.

**Table 3.9.** District error of all three estimates (RMSE, in points), and the
correlation between Model B and the certified result (`r_model_b`).

**Table 3.10.** Statewide Harris share from each estimate, against the certified
result, in percent.

```{r poststrat-b}
dr <- frame_class[vote2024 %in% c("D", "R")]
dr[, p_b := predict(m_b, newdata = dr, type = "response", allow.new.levels = TRUE)]
b_cd <- dr[, .(model_b = sum(N * p_b) / sum(N)), by = cd]
b_state <- dr[, sum(N * p_b) / sum(N)]

v <- merge(v, b_cd, by = "cd")
v[, .(rmse_weighted_avg = sqrt(mean((100 * (raw - certified))^2)),
      rmse_model_a      = sqrt(mean((100 * (model_a - certified))^2)),
      rmse_model_b      = sqrt(mean((100 * (model_b - certified))^2)),
      r_model_b         = cor(model_b, certified))]

data.table(estimate = c("weighted average (Notebook 2)", "Model A: census MrP", "Model B: stage-2 frame", "certified"),
           harris_2p = round(100 * c(raw_state, a_state, b_state, state_certified), 1))
```

In Table 3.9, Model B has the smallest district error of the three and a
correlation with the certified result of almost 1. In Table 3.10 all three
statewide estimates sit one to two points above the certified 44.3.

The last block plots all three estimates against the certified result, one
point per district and estimate, saves the plot to `figures/`, and shows it.

**Figure 3.2.** Your 400 twins against the certified 2024 result, by district:
weighted average (grey), Model A (red), Model B (blue, labelled by district).

```{r validate-plot, fig.height = 5}
long <- melt(v, id.vars = c("cd", "certified", "twins"), measure.vars = c("raw", "model_a", "model_b"),
             variable.name = "estimate", value.name = "twins_2p")
long[, estimate := factor(estimate, c("raw", "model_a", "model_b"),
                          c("Weighted average", "Model A: census MrP", "Model B: stage-2 frame"))]
p_mrp <- ggplot(long, aes(100 * certified, 100 * twins_2p, colour = estimate)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(size = 2.6) +
  geom_text(data = long[estimate == "Model B: stage-2 frame"], aes(label = sub("OH-", "", cd)),
            nudge_y = 1.8, size = 3, colour = "grey30", show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Weighted average" = "grey65", "Model A: census MrP" = "#c0504d",
                                 "Model B: stage-2 frame" = "#2c6e9e")) +
  labs(x = "Certified Harris share, two-party (%)", y = "Twins' Harris share, two-party (%)",
       colour = NULL, title = "Your 400 twins against the certified 2024 result, by district",
       subtitle = "Each point is one of Ohio's 15 districts") +
  coord_equal() + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
ggsave(file.path("..", "figures", "oh_mrp_vs_certified.png"), p_mrp, width = 8, height = 6, dpi = 200)
p_mrp
```

In Figure 3.2, the blue points (Model B) sit close to the dashed line, and the
red points (Model A) are squeezed towards the middle.

> **Discussion: why Model B's success is not evidence.** Model B lands close to
> the certified result. Now trace what went in, step by step:
>
> 1. each cell's D and R counts were **raked to that very result** (Notebook 1, Section 2);
> 2. each twin's donor was **matched on the class** of its cell (Notebook 2, Section 3);
> 3. so the donated attitudes the model read were chosen to fit that class, and
>    the model gave the class back almost every time (Notebook 2, Table 2.12);
> 4. Model B then weights those answers by the same raked class counts.
>
> Recovering 2024 therefore tests whether the pipeline **kept what it was
> given**. It says nothing about whether the twins can read an election. That is
> worth knowing, since a pipeline that lost its inputs would be broken, but it is
> a check on the plumbing. A recovery within a point or two is the pipeline
> working as designed.
>
> Evidence that twins can read an election needs an election that is in **no
> part** of the pipeline: not in the frame, the rake, the donors or the persona.
> If the twins get that one right, the calibration cannot be the reason. Section 7 has
> one: New Jersey, November 2025.

## 6. The 2026 Senate race

For 2026, Model B's structure is the useful one. It asks how each 2024 class,
within each census cell, votes in 2026, and weights the cells by the frame's
class counts. It needs two models, because who turns out is not given:

- a **turnout** model, fitted on every twin (the probability of voting at all);
- a **vote** model on Brown's two-party share, with each twin weighted by its
  own probability of voting.

Your twins have no third-party class, so the vote class enters as a random
intercept. The frame's small "Other" class (51,202 adults in Table 3.3, about
0.6% of Ohio) then gets the average.

The block below prints nothing. It adds two columns to `iv`: `turnout` (one
minus the `no_vote` probability) and `brown_2p` (Brown's share of the Brown +
Husted probability). It fits the turnout model (`m_turn`) and the vote model
(`m_vote`), and adds both predictions to every row of `frame_class` (`p_turn`,
`p_brown`). `brown_state` is Brown's share among expected voters in Ohio, and
`turnout_state` the expected turnout among adults.

```{r fit-2026}
iv[, `:=`(turnout = 1 - no_vote, brown_2p = dem / (dem + rep))]
f26 <- y ~ gender + college_grad + (1 | vote2024) + (1 | age_bins) + (1 | ethnicity) + (1 | cd)
m_turn <- fit(f26, stack(iv, iv$turnout))
m_vote <- fit(f26, stack(iv, iv$brown_2p, iv$turnout))
frame_class[, `:=`(p_turn  = predict(m_turn, newdata = frame_class, type = "response", allow.new.levels = TRUE),
                   p_brown = predict(m_vote, newdata = frame_class, type = "response", allow.new.levels = TRUE))]
brown_state   <- frame_class[, sum(N * p_turn * p_brown) / sum(N * p_turn)]
turnout_state <- frame_class[, sum(N * p_turn) / sum(N)]
```

The next block puts your twins' Brown share beside three comparisons: the
project's panel (its Ohio row in `benchmark_ohio.csv`; Section 7 shows all twelve panels);
the RealClearPolitics polling average of 8–9 September 2026 (Brown 48.8, Husted
45.5); and, as a baseline, Harris's certified 2024 share. It then prints the
turnout your twins imply.

**Table 3.11.** Brown's share of the two-party vote in 2026, in percent, from
four sources; then the turnout your twins imply.

```{r senate-compare}
# RealClearPolitics average of 8–9 September 2026, Brown 48.8 / Husted 45.5
POLL_BROWN_2P <- 48.8 / (48.8 + 45.5)
bench <- fread(file.path(DATA, "benchmark_ohio.csv"))[panel == "oh_statewide"]

data.table(
  source   = c("Your twins, MrP", "Talking to Machines panel, 4,000 registrants", "RCP polling average",
               "2024 baseline: certified Harris share"),
  brown_2p = round(100 * c(brown_state, bench$dem_2p_2026_llm / 100, POLL_BROWN_2P, state_certified), 1))
cat(sprintf("Turnout implied by your twins: %.1f%% of adults\n", 100 * turnout_state))
```

> **Discussion.** In Table 3.11, the project's twins give Brown 46.6 (the
> `Talking to Machines panel` row) and yours give him 47.3 (`Your twins, MrP`),
> both close to the 2024 baseline of 44.3, while the polls give him 51.7
> (`RCP polling average`). The persona carries 2024-era partisanship and issue positions and
> **nothing about 2026**: no national environment, no incumbency, no campaign,
> no Sherrod Brown crossover vote. A record-only twin is a *stable partisan
> baseline*, not a reading of the current race.

## 7. What the Talking to Machines panels show

Your panel is 400 synthetic twins. Talking to Machines builds panels of 4,000
real registrants each and interviews every one with the same vote module. Twelve
of them are shown here, in six states: Ohio, North Carolina, Pennsylvania,
Washington, New York and New Jersey.

> **Note on the data.** Only the Ohio files are public. The other states' panel
> results carry non-commercial terms, so they are not in this repository, and
> the blocks in this section run only when those files are present. The website
> version of this notebook shows their output.

The block below loads their results from `benchmark_12panels.csv` as a table
called `b`, and prints one row per panel. The New Jersey Senate race has no
public poll, so its 2026 poll and gap show a dash.

**Table 3.12.** The twelve panels. Each row is a **different panel**: twelve
different electorates, statewide or single-district, each compared with its
**own** benchmark. They are not twelve versions of the same thing. The first
three numeric columns are 2024: the certified Democratic two-party share
(`harris_certified`), the twins' recall of their own 2024 vote
(`harris_twins`), and the gap. The last three are 2026: the polling average for
that race (`polls_2026`), the twins' stated intention (`twins_2026`), and the
gap. All figures are in percent.

```{r benchmark, eval = PANELS}
b <- fread(file.path(DATA, "benchmark_12panels.csv"))
dash <- function(x) fifelse(is.na(x), "—", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1))   # no poll: shown as a dash, never filled
b[, .(panel = label, harris_certified = harris_2p_certified, harris_twins = harris_2p_twins, gap_2024,
      polls_2026 = dash(dem_2p_polls), twins_2026 = dem_2p_2026_llm, gap_2026 = dash(dem_2p_2026_llm - dem_2p_polls))]
```

The first row of Table 3.12, `OH Senate`, is the project's panel from Notebook 2,
Table 2.13. In the `gap_2024` column, ten of the twelve panels reproduce the
certified 2024 Democratic two-party share to within 2.6 points, and nine to
within 2; the largest error is 3.8 points, in New Jersey (`NJ Senate`). Against
2026 polling the picture is different, and consistently so. Of the eleven panels
with a poll, eight have a negative `gap_2026`, between 4.3 and 11.0 points below
the polls, and three sit above them, by 0.9 to 2.9 (`OH-09`, `WA-03`, `NY-17`).
The panels recover where the electorate has already been, and read more
Republican than the polls about where it is going.

The next block plots the same table: each panel appears twice, once for 2024
(blue: twins against the certified result) and once for 2026 (red: twins against
the polls).

**Figure 3.3.** The twelve panels: 2024 recall and 2026 intention against their
benchmarks.

```{r benchmark-plot, fig.height = 5, eval = PANELS}
bl <- rbind(b[, .(label, benchmark = harris_2p_certified, twins = harris_2p_twins, contest = "2024 recall vs certified")],
            b[!is.na(dem_2p_polls), .(label, benchmark = dem_2p_polls, twins = dem_2p_2026_llm, contest = "2026 intention vs polls")])
ggplot(bl, aes(benchmark, twins, colour = contest)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(size = 2.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#2c6e9e", "#c0504d")) +
  labs(x = "Benchmark, Democratic two-party share (%)", y = "Twins (%)", colour = NULL,
       title = "Twelve Talking to Machines panels: 2024 recall and 2026 intention",
       subtitle = "The 2024 recall sits near the line; the 2026 answer mostly sits below the polls") +
  coord_equal() + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

### A held-out election: New Jersey, November 2025

The 2024 result is *inside* the pipeline. The 4 November 2025 New Jersey
governor's race is in no part of it: not in the frame, the donors or the
persona. That makes it the real test.

The block below loads the test as `nj`, one row per New Jersey county: the
number of twins in the county (`n_twins`), the certified share for Mikie
Sherrill, the Democrat (`certified`), the twins' predicted share (`twins`), and
the gap. It prints two summaries across the 21 counties, then plots each county.

**Figure 3.4.** New Jersey 2025 governor, by county: twins against the certified
result. Above the plot, `r` is the correlation between the two, and `MAE` the
average miss in points, each county weighted by its twins.

```{r nj-counties, fig.height = 5, eval = PANELS}
nj <- fread(file.path(DATA, "nj2025_holdout_counties.csv"))
cat(sprintf("21 counties: r = %.3f, twin-weighted MAE %.1f points\n",
            nj[, cor(twins, certified)], nj[, sum(n_twins * abs(gap)) / sum(n_twins)]))
ggplot(nj, aes(certified, twins)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(aes(size = n_twins), colour = "#2c6e9e", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = county), nudge_y = 1.8, size = 2.8, colour = "grey30") +
  labs(x = "Certified Sherrill share, two-party (%)", y = "Twins' Sherrill share (%)", size = "twins",
       title = "New Jersey 2025 governor, by county: an election the twins never saw") +
  coord_equal() + theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

The geography is right: the counties in Figure 3.4 fall along the line, with a
correlation of 0.94, in an election the twins were never calibrated to.

The statewide level needs its own numbers, which the county file does not
give. The block below prints them: five statewide shares for New Jersey, three
for the 2025 governor's race and two for the 2024 presidential race, each with
where it comes from.

**Table 3.13.** New Jersey statewide, Democratic two-party share in percent
(`value_pct`): the twins against the certified result, in 2025 and in 2024.

```{r nj-statewide, eval = PANELS}
fread(file.path(DATA, "nj2025_holdout_headline.csv"))[, .(quantity, election, value_pct, source)]
```

The twins' 2025 share appears twice in Table 3.13, because a vote share depends
on who votes as well as on how they vote. `sherrill_share_twins` (57.3) counts
each twin's answer in proportion to the chance of voting the twin itself stated
in the interview. This is the number the panel gives on its own, before the
election. `sherrill_share_twins_actual_turnout` (56.6) counts only the twins
whose registrant did vote in November 2025, according to the voter file, which
can only be known afterwards. The second holds turnout at its true value, so it
measures vote choice alone. The 0.7 points between them are the twins' turnout
error showing up in the vote share; Table 3.14 below shows that error directly.
Both are within a point of the certified result, so the argument that follows
holds for either.

In Table 3.13 the project's panel gives Sherrill 57.3 (`sherrill_share_twins`),
or 56.6 counting only actual voters, against a certified 57.2
(`sherrill_share_certified`). That near-hit is **two errors cancelling**, not
accuracy. New Jersey is where the panels are weakest on 2024: in Table 3.12,
`NJ Senate` has the largest `gap_2024` of the twelve, 3.8 points too
Democratic, and it is the state where the CES donor pool is thinnest relative
to the state's registered Republicans. Table 3.13 shows the same bias, about 4
points: the twins recall 57.2 for Harris (`harris_share_twins`) against her
certified 53.0 (`harris_share_certified`). Table 3.13 comes from an earlier draw
of the New Jersey panel, which is why its recall differs slightly from Table
3.12. Then the electorate swung about 4 points Democratic in 2025, from Harris's
certified 53.0 to Sherrill's 57.2. The twins did not move; the electorate moved
onto them.

Turnout is where the twins fail. The block below prints the turnout test.

**Table 3.14.** New Jersey 2025 turnout, twins against the voter file. Each row
is a group of New Jersey twins with the same voting record: how many of the
five general elections from 2016 to 2024 the file shows them voting in
(`generals_voted_of_5`, from 0 to 5). For each group: the number of twins; the
share the twins themselves predicted would vote in November 2025
(`twins_predict`); the share of the same registrants who actually voted,
according to the file (`actually_voted`); and the difference (`error`). Shares
are in percent.

```{r nj-turnout, eval = PANELS}
fread(file.path(DATA, "nj2025_holdout_turnout_by_record.csv"))[
  , .(generals_voted_of_5 = grp, twins = n, twins_predict = llm, actually_voted = actual, error = gap)]
```

Read the `error` column of Table 3.14 from top to bottom. The two ends are right:
people who never vote, and people who always do, are off by 6 points or less.
The middle is rounded up to "regular voter": twins with one to four generals on
their record are predicted to vote 18 to 35 points more often than they did. The project's rule follows from this:
**take vote choice from the twin, take turnout from the voter file.**

---

## What to take away

1. **MrP is what turns 400 twins into Ohio**, but only as well as the frame
   knows what matters. A census-only frame knows demographics. Ohio's districts
   differ politically, so census MrP shrinks them together.
2. **Recovering 2024 is not validation.** The stage-2 frame and the donor match
   were both calibrated to it, so Model B gets it right largely by construction.
3. **A record-only twin is a stable partisan baseline.** It does not know the
   2026 environment, and the gap to the polls is the size of that environment.
4. **The structure is real; the level needs care.** Geography holds up on an
   election the twins never saw. Level accuracy in any one election depends on
   knowing both the panel's baseline bias and the swing.

## Where this comes from

The twelve panels and the New Jersey held-out test come from the digital-twin
work of **Talking to Machines**, an international collaboration of academics and
industry researchers directed by Sonja Vogt (HEC Lausanne) and Ray Duch
(Nuffield College, Oxford).
